statement.p:
This activity demonstrates how to determine the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace of \real^m.
Let's begin by considering a line L, defined by the vector \wvec=\twovec21, and a vector \bvec=\twovec24 not on L, as illustrated in .
A two dimensional line, a vector not on the line, and its orthogonal complement.
A two dimensional vector \wvec defines a line L. There is a vector \bvec not on L as well as its orthogonal projection \bhat onto the line and the difference \bvec-\bhat.
The orthogonal projection is now represented as a scalar multiple of a basis vector for the line.
This diagram contains most of the same key features as the previous diagram. There is a vector \wvec that defines the line L, a vector \bvec not on line, and the orthogonal projection of \bvec onto L. The key difference is that the orthogonal projection \bhat is written as s\wvec, a scalar multiple of \wvec. In this way, the vector \bvec-\bhat = \bvec-s\wvec is orthogonal to L, which provides a means of finding s and hence \bhat.
Finding the orthogonal projection of \bvec onto the line defined by \wvec.
To find \bhat, first notice that \bhat = s\wvec for some scalar s. Since \bvec-\bhat = \bvec - s\wvec is orthogonal to \wvec, what do we know about the dot product
(\bvec-s\wvec)\cdot\wvec\text{?}
Apply the distributive property of dot products to find the scalar s. What is the vector \bhat, the orthogonal projection of \bvec onto L?
More generally, explain why the orthogonal projection of \bvec onto the line defined by \wvec is
\bhat= \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec}{\wvec\cdot\wvec}~\wvec\text{.}
The same ideas apply more generally. Suppose we have an orthogonal set of vectors \wvec_1=\threevec22{-1} and \wvec_2=\threevec102 that define a plane W in \real^3. If \bvec=\threevec396 another vector in \real^3, we seek the vector \bhat on the plane W closest to \bvec. As before, the vector \bvec-\bhat will be orthogonal to W, as illustrated in .
Finding the orthogonal projection in three dimensions.
Two orthogonal three dimensional vectors \wvec_1 and \wvec_2 define a plane W. There is a vector \bvec not on the plane and its orthogonal projection \bhat onto W. The vector \bvec-\bhat is drawn as a vector orthogonal to W.
Given a plane W defined by the orthogonal vectors \wvec_1 and \wvec_2 and another vector \bvec, we seek the vector \bhat on W closest to \bvec.
The vector \bvec-\bhat is orthogonal to W. What does this say about the dot products: (\bvec-\bhat)\cdot\wvec_1 and (\bvec-\bhat)\cdot\wvec_2?
Since \bhat is in the plane W, we can write it as a linear combination \bhat = c_1\wvec_1 + c_2\wvec_2. Then
\bvec-\bhat = \bvec - (c_1\wvec_1+c_2\wvec_2)\text{.}
Find the weight c_1 by dotting \bvec-\bhat with \wvec_1 and applying the distributive property of dot products. Similarly, find the weight c_2.
What is the vector \bhat, the orthogonal projection of \bvec onto the plane W?
Suppose that W is a subspace of \real^m with orthogonal basis \wvec_1,\wvec_2,\ldots,\wvec_n and that \bvec is a vector in \real^m. Explain why the orthogonal projection of \bvec onto W is the vector
\bhat = \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_1}{\wvec_1\cdot\wvec_1}~\wvec_1 + \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_2}{\wvec_2\cdot\wvec_2}~\wvec_2 + \cdots + \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_n}{\wvec_n\cdot\wvec_n}~\wvec_n\text{.}
Suppose that \uvec_1,\uvec_2,\ldots,\uvec_n is an orthonormal basis for W; that is, the vectors are orthogonal to one another and have unit length. Explain why the orthogonal projection is
\bhat= (\bvec\cdot\uvec_1)~\uvec_1 + (\bvec\cdot\uvec_2)~\uvec_2 + \cdots + (\bvec\cdot\uvec_n)~\uvec_n\text{.}
If Q=\begin{bmatrix} \uvec_1 \amp \uvec_2 \amp \ldots \amp \uvec_n \end{bmatrix} is the matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis of W, use to explain why \bhat = QQ^T\bvec.

li.p: This dot product should be 0 since the vectors are orthogonal.
We know \bhat=c_1\wvec_1 + c_2\wvec_2 + \cdots + c_n\wvec_n and we can find c_i=\frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_i}{\wvec_i\cdot\wvec_i} by requiring that \bvec-\bhat be orthogonal to every vector \wvec_i.
The vectors \uvec_i form an orthogonal set and since \uvec_i\cdot\uvec_i = \len{\uvec_i}^2 = 1, the weights are c_i=\frac{\bvec\cdot\uvec_i}{\uvec_i\cdot\uvec_i} = \bvec\cdot\uvec_i.

We have Q^T\bvec = \cthreevec{\bvec\cdot\uvec_1}{\vdots}{\bvec\cdot\uvec_n} so that QQ^T\bvec = (\bvec\cdot\uvec_1)~\uvec_1 + (\bvec\cdot\uvec_2)~\uvec_2 + \cdots + (\bvec\cdot\uvec_n)~\uvec_n=\bhat\text{.}
We require that \bvec-\bhat be orthogonal to every vector \wvec_i.
